title: Looking back: the code

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Tenth Guru's pen: his lines in the morning prayers, the Ardas and the amrit. Your line was pen and sword. Did a moment ask for a gentle word and a firm one at once? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

Across a park lawn runs a strip of bare dirt where the grass gave up. Planners have a name for it: a desire line. Nobody drew it on a map. Feet made it, one person after another, choosing the same way until the way was visible. A way of life can grow like that. It can also be written down, so that the next person doesn't have to guess where the path runs. For a long stretch of this year we walked through one written way, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a section at a time. Today we look back at the whole of it, and at why it's fair to call it a way.
screen: `A STRIP OF BARE DIRT ACROSS THE GRASS.` → `FEET MADE THE PATH.` → `A WAY, WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the code's shape. After it answers who a Sikh is, it sorts Sikh living into two sides: a Sikh's personal life, and the life of the panth, the community together. Everything we met this year hangs on one side or the other. Second, look at what the personal side rests on. In paraphrase, the code names three things: meditating on the Name and the scriptures, living by the Gurus' teaching, and serving others. Not first a journey, not first a uniform. The Name, the conduct, the service. Ordinary things, kept every day. The panth side is where the shared shape lives: the sangat and the gurdwara, the langar, the amrit and the Khalsa's discipline, and the ways the community settles questions together. Third, why the two sides belong together. The code's daily pattern leans on a passage by Guru Ram Das that we met early in that block. In paraphrase: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name, and keeps the Guru's word through the day. Then the passage turns. Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. One person's morning, and then the turn toward others. A code takes that pattern and makes it specific enough to share, so that strangers can walk it side by side. Fourth, nobody walks a whole path at once. The booklet holds a lifetime of practice, but a day is kept one practice at a time: a morning prayer, a covered head, a shared meal, an hour of seva. Step by step, the way stops being a page and becomes a path, worn in by the people who walk it.
screen: `TWO SIDES: PERSONAL AND PANTH.` · `NAME, CONDUCT, SERVICE.` · `GURU RAM DAS: A SIKH'S DAY.` · `ONE PRACTICE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one practice, right now. Settle, and breathe. Choose one of the code's three. The Name: if you like, repeat Waheguru quietly with each breath. The Gurus' teaching: bring back one line of theirs you met this year, and ask how you'd live it today. Service: think of one person you could serve today, and see the first small step clearly. Choose just one, and stay with it. If your mind wanders, come back to the same one. If you pray, this can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today, at the code: a written way, with a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time. Today's word.
Your line: the way. Today, keep the one practice you chose once more, at a set time, as if your feet were wearing in a path. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs look to the Sikh Rehat Maryada for a shared pattern of personal practice, such as the daily prayers, Naam and seva, and of congregational life in the gurdwara, the langar and the amrit.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rehat, the Sikh way of living, as in Rehat Maryada, the code.

trapdoor: what you thought: a code is a rulebook of things you can't do.
what it means: the Rehat Maryada lays out a shared way, with a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time.
what a scholar hears: its personal side rests on Naam and the scriptures, the Gurus' teaching and seva, echoing Guru Ram Das's picture of a Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it.
